prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Once I believed in you; I planted a fig tree. Here, in Vermont, country of no summer. It was a test: if the tree lived, it would mean you existed. By this logic, you do not exist. Or you exist exclusively in warmer climates, in fervent Sicily and Mexico and California, where are grown the unimaginable apricot and fragile peach. Perhaps they see your face in Sicily; here we barely see the hem of your garment. I have to discipline myself to share with John and Noah the tomato crop. If there is justice in some other world, those like myself, whom nature forces into lives of abstinence, should get the lion's share of all things, all objects of hunger, greed being praise of you. And no one praises more intensely than I, with more painfully checked desire, or more deserves to sit at your right hand, if it exists, partaking of the perishable, the immortal fig, which does not travel.

Here are a few ways to polish the passage, depending on the exact tone you wish to achieve while preserving all original details and philosophical depth.

### Option 1: Elevated & Elegant Literary Prose
*This option refines the rhythm and vocabulary while maintaining the poetic, intimate quality of the original.*

> There was a time when I believed in you, and so I planted a fig tree here in Vermont—a land virtually devoid of summer. It was meant as a test: if the tree survived, it would prove your existence. By that logic, you do not exist. Or perhaps your presence belongs exclusively to warmer climates—to the fervent realms of Sicily, Mexico, and California, where the unimaginable apricot and delicate peach flourish. Perhaps in Sicily they behold your face; here, we catch barely a glimpse of the hem of your garment. I must discipline myself even to share our tomato harvest with John and Noah. 
> 
> If justice exists in another world, then those of us whom nature compels into lives of austerity ought to receive the lion’s share of all things—every object of longing—for intense desire is itself a form of praise. And no one praises you more fervently than I, with a desire so painfully restrained. No one is more deserving to sit at your right hand—should such a place exist—and partake in the perishable, immortal fig, a treasure that cannot endure travel.

---

### Option 2: Sophisticated & Formal 
*This option uses slightly more structured, classic prose, making it sound authoritative, reflective, and deeply resonant.*

> Once, as an act of faith, I planted a fig tree in Vermont—a place starved of summer. It served as a crucible: the tree’s survival would confirm your existence. By this measure, you are absent. Alternatively, you exist solely in gentler climes—in the vibrant warmth of Sicily, Mexico, and California, where exotic apricots and fragile peaches thrive. While the people of Sicily may see your face, we in this harsh landscape catch scarcely the hem of your garment. It requires deliberate self-restraint for me even to share the tomato crop with John and Noah. 
> 
> Should ultimate justice prevail in some other realm, those like myself, whom nature forces into lives of abstinence, deserve the lion’s share of all earthly desires—for true longing is the highest praise of your creation. Indeed, no one praises you with greater intensity or more painfully suppressed desire than I; none are more worthy to sit at your right hand—if it exists—and savor the delicate, immortal fig, a fruit too fragile to travel.

---

### Key Enhancements Made:
*   **Flow & Cadence:** Transitions between sentences (such as the shift from the test to the conclusion about warmer climates) were smoothed for better readability.
*   **Precision:** Words like "fervent" and "fragile" were paired thoughtfully to heighten the contrast between the cold climate of Vermont and the abundance of warmer regions.
*   **Tone Balance:** Maintained the underlying tension between spiritual devotion, physical scarcity, and bitter desire without changing any of the underlying narrative.

Here is a complete, well-structured essay expanding on those ideas:

***

In my youth, I attempted a small theological experiment: I planted a fig tree in the unforgiving soil of Vermont. I wanted to see if divine providence would bend the frost to its will and coax sweet, Mediterranean fruit from a landscape defined by long, bitter winters. The sapling, predictably, withered and died long before the arrival of spring. From its frozen decay, I drew a stark conclusion about the nature of the divine. God, it seemed to me, was entirely absent from these brutal northern reaches. The Almighty was a deity of warmth and sunlight, existing only in fertile regions where abundance flows effortlessly and the earth yields its bounty without a struggle.

Living under the weight of this severe climate leaves no room for casual ease. Here, the relentless cold forces a life of strict discipline and painstaking restraint. Every piece of firewood, every store of grain, and every spark of warmth must be guarded with fierce vigilance. Scarcity is our constant companion, compelling us to manage our limited resources with absolute precision. To survive in such an environment is to practice a daily, unspoken asceticism, stripping away all desire for comfort until only bare endurance remains.

Yet, this prolonged hardship has shaped my understanding of cosmic justice. It would be fundamentally unfair for those who bask in easy, climate-blessed warmth to inherit the same eternity as those who endure the freezing dark. I have come to believe that those of us forced into earthly deprivation deserve the lion’s share of rewards in the afterlife. The scales must eventually balance; those who suffered through nature's harshness on Earth are rightfully entitled to the greatest treasures of heaven, far surpassing any paradise granted to those who knew only comfort in life.

Ultimately, true piety is not found in enjoying the easy gifts of a gentle climate, but in the painful mastery of one's own longings. To ache for warmth and sweet fruit, yet to suppress that desire and endure the frost, represents the highest form of spiritual devotion. It requires no faith to praise God when the sun shines and the branches are heavy with figs. True divine favor is earned in the bitter cold, where painfully suppressed desire becomes a living sacrifice, proving a devotion far deeper than any easy abundance could ever produce.
outputs.L4:
In the high, frost-pocked hills of Vermont, where summer often feels less like a season and more like a brief, hesitant pause between winters, the earth does not easily yield to metaphors of abundance. It was here, amidst the granite outcroppings and damp, unyielding shade, that I set out to perform a quiet theological test. I purchased a sapling of a Mediterranean fig—a creature of dust, heat, and sun-drenched antiquity—and planted it deeply into the cold northern soil. It was an act of deliberate folly, but also a calculated spiritual experiment: a test to see if the divine creator, so often envisioned as a source of warm, overflowing grace, possessed a presence that could reach into a landscape so stubbornly barren.

I tended to the sapling with meticulous care, building windbreaks against the biting mountain gales and monitoring the soil’s bitter moisture. I wanted to see if faith, paired with human labor, could coax a miracle of warmth out of an unforgiving climate. But the environment offered no concessions. The summer proved brief and overcast; the sun remained a pale, distant coin behind blanketed clouds. Before the autumn had even properly arrived, an early, blackening frost descended upon the valley. The fig tree’s broad, delicate leaves curled, turned translucent, and died without ever bearing fruit. The experiment was over.

Looking at the withered stem sticking out of the frozen earth, the conclusion was inescapable. The traditional god of scriptures—the god of milk, honey, and sun-ripened fruit—was absent from these cold northern lands. If a divine presence governed the Mediterranean cradle where the fig first flourished, it had clearly drawn a boundary at the latitude of our perpetual cold. In Vermont, nature operated under a law of stoic indifference, untouched by the warm breath of a compassionate creator.

Yet, out of this recognized absence emerged a harder, more profound truth. To live in a summerless climate is to practice a form of ascetic devotion. The people who inhabit these northern reaches do not enjoy the easy, unearned mercies of a gentle climate; instead, they endure a forced, natural deprivation. They are shaped by a disciplined longing—a capacity to love the sun precisely because it vanishes, and to maintain an appetite for life in an environment that constantly threatens to extinguish it.

If divine justice exists anywhere in the cosmos, it cannot belong to those who bask in easy warmth, harvesting fruit they did nothing to coax from a benevolent soil. Instead, the ultimate share of grace and reward must belong to the survivors of the cold. It is those who endure the long, grey silences of the north—who cultivate hope without the promise of a harvest—who hold the true claim to justice. Their discipline is their testament, and in their unrequited longing, they become the most deserving of whatever paradise might eventually answer their patience.
outputs.L5:
**Once**, I believed that peace was something you had to build with sheer willpower, brick by brick, against the tide of a restless world. I spent years chasing the horizon, moving through crowded cities where the night sky was washed out by electric light, always searching for a quiet corner to breathe. 

It wasn’t until a crisp October afternoon, cresting a hill on a back road lined with crimson sugar maples, that I realized peace isn’t constructed—it is found. 

That was my introduction to **Vermont**. 

There is a timeless grace to this state, where history rests gently against the hillsides and the rhythm of life is dictated by the turning of the seasons. In the spring, the woods come alive with the steady drip of maple sap. Summer brings emerald ridges and cold mountain streams, while winter covers the quiet valleys in a blanket of blue-tinted snow. Covered bridges stand like wooden guardians over rushing water, and small towns anchor themselves around white-steepled churches and bustling general stores. 

**Here**, nestled in the shadow of the Green Mountains, the world finally slows down. **Here**, the air carries the scent of pine and woodsmoke, and the silence isn't empty; it is rich with the whisper of the wind through ancient trees and the distant call of a loon across a glassy pond. 

**Once**, I was just a traveler passing through, looking for a temporary escape. But standing **here** today, watching the fog roll gently over the Vermont hills, I realize I didn't just find a beautiful landscape—I found a place to call home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue in the style of Louise Glück about testing God's existence by trying to plant a fig tree in the cold climate of Vermont.
counterfactuals.output:
I planted the Mediterranean here,
in the slate soil of Washington County,
where autumn is not a season 
but an execution.

A fig tree. A small, pale stick
with broad leaves like hands outstretched,
asking for what this earth has never known:
an endless afternoon,
the heavy, golden air of a warmer world.

I said to you: *If you are there,
keep this tender thing alive.*

It was not a prayer. It was a wager.
I wanted proof that you were not merely
the architect of frost,
that you possessed a capacity for mercy
that exceeded the climate.

All winter I watched the snow pile
against the burlap I bound around its trunk.
I wrapped it tightly, the way one wraps a dead child,
so the wind could not touch the skin.
I left it in the dark with you. 

You prefer the hemlock, don't you?
The granite, the harsh birch,
the black pine that starves itself into beauty.
You prefer the things that ask nothing of you,
that accept the ice as a natural law.

In May, when the thaw finally came—
reluctant, grey, smelling of wet stone—
I knelt in the cold mud.
I untied the twine. I cut back the cloth.

The wood was snap-dry. Black at the core.
No pale green beneath the skin.

You answered me, of course. 
You always answer.
You spoke in the only language you allow the ground:
*Nothing strays from its place.*
*Nothing survives my order.*

And I stood up, wiping the dirt from my knees,
satisfied, at last, 
by the precise cruelty of your truth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a passage from the perspective of an austere gardener who argues that self-denial and unfulfilled desire are the ultimate forms of divine praise.
counterfactuals.output:
The novice enters the sanctuary of soil and mistakes vulgar abundance for grace. He swoons over the heavy, overripe plum dropping from the bough; he celebrates the rose that splits its sepals to spill its voluptuous, fleeting perfume upon the air. They are mistaken, all of them. The world believes the garden praises the Creator through its overflow. I tell you, it praises Him best through its restraint.

To bloom is to expend. It is an act of vanity, a brief and noisy climax that ends in rot. When a flower opens fully, it has surrendered its mystery; it has spent its yearning. It is finished. But the bud—tight, hard, and trembling in the November frost, held back by the cold and the severity of my shears—that is a prayer uninterrupted. 

Look to the vine in times of drought. When the rains are plentiful, the plant grows fat and soft; its roots lie lazy near the surface, satisfied with cheap grace. But deny it water, strip away its eager suckers, and watch what transpires. Its roots will tear through slate and granite, driving down into the cold, black depths of the earth to seek the hidden springs. It is the ache of thirst that makes the root strong. It is the denial of the surface that compels the descent into the divine dark.

What higher praise can a creature offer the Almighty than an unquenched hunger? To be full is to turn one’s back on Heaven, to say, *I have enough.* But to live in the taut, exquisite tension of unfulfilled desire—to feel the holy fire of wanting and to deliberately withhold the hand from the fruit—that is adoration in its purest state. 

Every winter, I walk these stone paths with my iron shears. I cut away the promising shoots. I pinch back the early buds that dare to dream of summer. I do not do this out of cruelty, but out of a rigorous love. I am teaching the earth how to fast. I am keeping the garden in a state of perpetual, burning readiness. 

The highest altar is not the table laid with a feast, but the empty soil that waits, suffering and pure, refusing to consume itself in lesser joys. God does not dwell in the satisfaction of our appetites, but in the clean, cavernous space made by our refusal. My garden does not shout its devotion in colorful, dying blooms. It whispers it in unspent strength, in pruned limbs, in the magnificent, quiet sanctity of all it has chosen not to become.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: We buried the pale sapling in late October, forcing its tender roots into granite-heavy Vermont soil just as the green hills stripped down to gray bones. It felt like a foolish, sun-starved prayer. In Palermo or Ojai, the fig does not beg for light; it splits the volcanic ash of Sicily and drinks the thick Pacific haze of California, bending low under dark, split-bellied fruit that bleeds honey onto scorching stone. There, warmth is an ancient inheritance. But here, life is a harsh negotiation with the frost. Before the first blizzard, we swaddled the sapling in burlap and straw, building a crude sarcophagus against thirty-below winds, burying a Mediterranean dream beneath the snow. counterfactuals.prompt: Write a bitter prayer from a gardener struggling with their yield, arguing that those forced into lives of restraint and cold deserve the lion's share of eternal rewards.
counterfactuals.output:
Lord of the Blighted Leaf and the Grudging Stone,

Look down at this dirt. Look at what my knuckles have paid to it, and look at what it has paid me back. 

I gave you sun-up to dusk. I gave you a spine bent like a weeping willow and hands split open like dry winter bark. I buried the seed deep, I watered it with sweat when the heavens turned to iron, and what did you let rise from the furrow? Thistles. Stunted turnip bulbs no bigger than plums, and rot in the heart of the squash. The frost came early, like a thief you invited into my field, while the wind howled through the gaps in my ribs.

I am tired of singing hymns over barren soil.

Down in the valley, the soft-handed men sit behind glass windows. They do not know the bite of the November mud through thin boots. They never had to choose between saving the seed-corn for spring or eating it to stop the cramping in their guts. Their trees break beneath the weight of peaches; their wheat grows straight and thick without them ever having to beg the sky for rain. They live in warmth, fat on ease, calling their good fortune your "grace."

If that is grace, then your justice had better be a terrible thing.

Hear me, Lord, from this frozen patch of earth: I keep a ledger. Every frostbitten finger, every meal of boiled weeds, every hour spent shivering over a harvest that failed before it began—it is all written down. We did not choose this austerity; it was beaten into us by your seasons. We were *forced* into this restraint, locked out in the cold while others feasted at the midsummer table.

So when the final winter closes my eyes, do not dare divide your paradise equally. 

The well-fed have had their heaven. They drank it warm from silver cups while they lived. They have used up their share of light. But us? The ones who coaxed nothing from the rocks? The ones who froze in the shadows of their bounty? 

The lion’s share belongs to us. 

Give the valley-dwellers the scraps of eternity—they know the taste of abundance already. But hand the keys of the kingdom to the bruised and the shivering. Crown the ones who starved in the dark, for we are the only ones who have paid for the feast in advance. 

Remember the cold you gave me, Lord. And remember what you owe.

Amen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary text exploring faith, geography, and the idea that greed born of scarcity is actually a intense form of devotion to God.
counterfactuals.output:
In the high, chalk-white badlands of the Salt Reaches, geography was not a background for life; it was an altar upon which life was continually bled. 

Here, the earth did not yield; it surrendered nothing without a tear. The wind blew thin and dry, smelling of pulverized limestone and ancient, dried sea-bed. The people who lived in the village of Oakhaven—a misnomer, for no tree had grown there in three generations—did not speak of God as a father or a shepherd. A shepherd implies green pastures, and green was a color forgotten by all but the oldest dying eyes. In the Reaches, God was the Great Ironist, the One who had hidden the marrow so deep within the bone of the earth that only the frantic, clawing fingers of the desperate could ever touch It.

Old Malachi sat in the cellar beneath his stone hut, his fingers caked in gray silt. Before him lay three earthen jars, sealed with pitch. Inside were seven measures of wild barley—the last of the spring harvest—and a leather skin containing four pints of brackish, iron-tasting water drawn from the deep seam in the basalt ridge.

Outside, the wind howled through the dry gullies, carrying the sound of a coughing child. Malachi did not move. He pressed his knees tighter against his chest, clutching the neck of the water skin with both hands, his knuckles white and polished like bird bones.

A soft knocking rattled the cedar door at the top of the stairs. 

"Father Malachi," a voice called. It was Jonah, the young deacon who had come from the southern valleys two years ago, still soft-skinned, still smelling faintly of river-mud and sweet grass. "The woman Mara’s babe is dry. Her milk has turned to chalk. One cup, Malachi. For the child’s throat."

Malachi did not answer. He closed his eyes and inhaled the damp, dark smell of his tiny, hoarded treasury. His teeth were clenched so hard his jaw throbbed.

"Malachi!" Jonah’s voice cracked. "It is a sin to hoard the gift of the earth while the innocent perish! God demands mercy!"

Malachi spat into the dry dust between his boots. *Mercy,* he thought. *The morality of the riverlands.*

When Jonah’s footsteps finally faded into the scraping wind, Malachi leaned his head against the cold clay of the jar. He was not cruel. He did not hate the child, nor did he take pleasure in Mara’s weeping. But Jonah understood nothing of the holy arithmetic of the Reaches. Jonah had grown up where rain fell like lazy blessings, where men gave away loaves because tomorrow the wheat would grow again. In the riverlands, generosity was easy, cheap, and shallow. It was a worship of abundance.

But here, in this geometry of stones and sky, abundance was a lie. Here, God was revealed only in the smallness of things.

Malachi pressed his lips to the leather skin. He did not drink. To drink would be to consume it, to end the miracle. He merely felt the cool, heavy pressure of the liquid inside. 

To Malachi, his greed was not a failing of the flesh; it was the highest, most agonizing form of prayer. 

In a land where God withheld Himself—where He hid His waters in the deepest bowels of the stone and buried His greenness under leagues of burning dust—to be generous was to blaspheme. To give away the water was to treat it as common, as worthless, as something that could be spared. It was an insult to the terrifying difficulty of its creation. 

Only the greedy man understood the true value of God’s work. Only the miser, counting his seeds in the dark with trembling, blood-flecked hands, knew the exact weight of a divine gift. 

When Malachi clutched his grain, he did not see wealth; he saw the light of Creation trapped in a husk. He loved that grain with a violent, jealous adoration that no full-bellied man of the valleys could ever comprehend. He loved it so much it made his ribs ache. He hoarded it because to let it go—to let it be consumed, digested, and turned into momentary warmth and urine—was to profane the terrible effort it took the sun and the stone to make it.

He opened his hand. A single grain of wild barley rested in his calloused palm, gray and withered. 

"Lord," Malachi whispered into the dark of the cellar. His voice was a dry rasp, like two stones grinding together. "Look how I hold it. Look how I do not waste what You have made."

His eyes watered, not from pity, but from the ecstatic terror of possession. He knew the geography of his land had shaped his soul. A flat, wet land made soft, watery souls that bled themselves out in easy pity. But this jagged, calcified mountain—this dry wilderness—demanded a soul carved of the same flint. It demanded an avarice so absolute that it mirrored the hard, withholding silence of Heaven itself.

God had not rained manna upon the Reaches. He had forced them to dig for it with their bare fingernails. Therefore, every grain was a relic, every drop of water a drop of the Creator's own blood. And how could one give away the blood of God to be swallowed down in a second of blind hunger?

No. The grain must be guarded. It must be loved, lusted after, wept over, and kept.

Upstairs, the wind shrieked, tearing at the thatched roof, trying to pull the village down into the dry dust. Malachi pulled the pitch-sealed jar closer, wrapping his old arms around the rough clay, pressing his cheek against it until he could feel the cold stillness within.

Out in the desert, God was hiding. And here in the dark, Malachi held Him fast, gripping Him with bleeding fingers, refusing to let Him go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
